BE NICE:
The individuals presented in these videos may be suffering from the effects of alcohol, drug abuse, a mental health disorder or simply having a bad day. The videos should NOT be presumed to be representative of their general behavior. Everyone deserves to be treated with respect. 

RIGHT TO BE FORGOTTEN:
Midwest Safety practices the "Right to be Forgotten." If you were the suspect in a lower-level offense, you may email our board to request removal.

The suspect driving the stolen jeep, Tyrone Griffin, who was 17 years old at the time of the crash, pleaded guilty in connection with the Euclid police pursuit that resulted in the death of 44-year-old Michelle Wall. Wall was on her way to church when the stolen Jeep driven by Tyrone Griffin struck her vehicle at a high rate of speed, ejecting her from the car. Medics later pronounced her dead at the scene. Griffin entered guilty pleas to one count of attempted murder and one count of failure to comply with the order or signal of a police officer. He was sentenced to 14 years in prison. A firearm was recovered from the stolen jeep, which had been taken during a carjacking involving two women in Cleveland on March 15th. Neither victim reported injuries from the initial carjacking. The word routine does not exist in police. A stolen car check and at gunpoint isn't just a piece of property. It's a loaded weapon racing down the city streets. And when the person driving is a juvenile, the danger multiplies and youth doesn't erase the risk. It amplifies it because impulse and horsepower made for a deadly combination. And I know firsthand that criminals, behind the will do not calculate consequences. They don't see people driving home for work or just people going to church. An impact is unforgiven because one second of reckless flight can erase an entire life in the blink of an eye. And that's the part of the public doesn't like to confront and honestly, I understand why. And a single pursuit decision isn't just about the suspect and squad cars. It's about the unknown people on the road who never acts to be a part of it in the first place. Now, learning that cops live in that contradiction. Pursuit too aggressively and you risk tragedy. You hold back and you allow a violent suspect to slip away only to strike a game later. There's no clean outcome when the suspect is a juvenile willing to play with lives that don't belong to him. So my question is, does age excuse the devastation left behind because a stolen car doesn't care if his driver is 16 or 36? Because the results are the same and the destruction just as final.
